title: Bekhorot 37
description: The close of chapter five, on who counts as a Sage for vows, a firstborn sold before it was shown to an expert and what the seller must refund, and the opening of chapter six, on the blemishes of the ear: torn cartilage, a split, a hole the size of a bitter vetch, and a desiccated ear.
topics: 🧑‍⚖️ Three laymen for a firstborn and for vows: “one such as me,” says Rav Naḥman
🥩 Firstborn meat sold before it was shown to a Sage, and a tereifa cow sold as kosher
💰 Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar: what one is repulsed by is refunded in full; the rest is reduced by its benefit
📖 Chapter 6 opens: a damaged, split, pierced or desiccated ear
🔎 Generalization, detail, generalization: exposed and permanent blemishes, but not hidden or temporary ones
👂 An awl, a thorn or a needle: piercing the Hebrew slave’s ear, and “here for slaughtering, there for disqualifying”
🫘 A bitter vetch that enters and exits, and Rav Ḥisda’s question on the skull and the sela

a1.he: לְאַפּוֹקֵי מִדְּרַבִּי יוֹסֵי, שְׁלֹשָׁה מְפִירִין אֶת הַנֶּדֶר בִּמְקוֹם שֶׁאֵין חָכָם לְאַפּוֹקֵי מִדְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה, דְּתַנְיָא: הֲפָרַת נְדָרִים בִּשְׁלֹשָׁה, רַבִּי יְהוּדָה אוֹמֵר: אֶחָד מֵהֶם חָכָם.

a2.he: בִּמְקוֹם שֶׁאֵין חָכָם. כְּגוֹן מַאן? אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן: כְּגוֹן אֲנָא. רַבִּי יְהוּדָה אוֹמֵר: אֶחָד מֵהֶן חָכָם, מִכְּלָל דְּהָנָךְ כֹּל דְּהוּ? אָמַר רָבִינָא: דְּמַסְבְּרִי לֵיהּ וְסָבַר.

a3.he: רַבִּי יוֹסֵי אוֹמֵר: אֲפִילּוּ יֵשׁ שָׁם עֶשְׂרִים וּשְׁלֹשָׁה כּוּ׳. אָמַר רַב חֲנַנְאֵל אָמַר רַב: אֵין הֲלָכָה כְּרַבִּי יוֹסֵי. פְּשִׁיטָא, יָחִיד וְרַבִּים הֲלָכָה כְּרַבִּים! מַהוּ דְּתֵימָא נִמּוּקוֹ עִמּוֹ? קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן.

a4.he: תִּפְשׁוֹט מֵהָא, דְּהָךְ קַמַּיְיתָא מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דִּשְׁמוּאֵל אִיתְּמַר, דְּאִי מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּרַב — תַּרְתֵּי לְמָה לִי?

a6.he: מַתְנִי׳ הַשּׁוֹחֵט אֶת הַבְּכוֹר, וְנוֹדַע שֶׁלֹּא הֶרְאָהוּ — מַה שֶּׁאָכְלוּ אָכְלוּ, וְיַחְזִיר לָהֶם הַדָּמִים, וּמַה שֶּׁלֹּא אָכְלוּ — הַבָּשָׂר יִקָּבֵר, וְיַחְזִיר אֶת הַדָּמִים.

a7.he: וְכֵן הַשּׁוֹחֵט אֶת הַפָּרָה וּמְכָרָהּ, וְנוֹדַע שֶׁהִיא טְרֵפָה — מַה שֶּׁאָכְלוּ אָכְלוּ, וּמַה שֶּׁלֹּא אָכְלוּ — הֵם יַחֲזִירוּ לוֹ אֶת הַבָּשָׂר, וְהוּא יַחֲזִיר לָהֶם אֶת הַדָּמִים. מְכָרוּהוּ לְגוֹיִם, אוֹ הִטִּילוּהוּ לִכְלָבִים — יְשַׁלְּמוּ דְּמֵי טְרֵפָה.

a8.he: גְּמָ׳ תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: הַמּוֹכֵר בָּשָׂר לַחֲבֵירוֹ וְנִמְצָא בְּשַׂר בְּכוֹר, פֵּירוֹת וְנִמְצָא טְבָלִים, יַיִן וְנִמְצָא יֵין נֶסֶךְ — מַה שֶּׁאָכְלוּ אָכְלוּ, וְיַחְזִיר לָהֶם אֶת הַדָּמִים.

a9.he: רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן אֶלְעָזָר אוֹמֵר: דְּבָרִים שֶׁהַנֶּפֶשׁ קָצָה בָּהֶן — יַחֲזִיר לָהֶן אֶת הַדָּמִים, וְשֶׁאֵין הַנֶּפֶשׁ קָצָה בָּהֶם — יְנַכֶּה לָהֶם אֶת הַדָּמִים. וְאֵלּוּ הֵן דְּבָרִים שֶׁהַנֶּפֶשׁ קָצָה בָּהֶן: נְבֵילוֹת וּטְרֵיפוֹת, שְׁקָצִים וּרְמָשִׂים. וְאֵלּוּ הֵן דְּבָרִים שֶׁאֵין הַנֶּפֶשׁ קָצָה בָּהֶן: בְּכוֹרוֹת, טְבָלִים וְיֵין נֶסֶךְ.

a11.he: לָא צְרִיכָא, כְּגוֹן דְּזַבֵּין לֵיהּ מִמְּקוֹם מוּמָא, דַּאֲמַר לֵיהּ: אִי לָאו דְּאָכְלַתְּ הֲוָה מַחְזֵינָא לֵיהּ וְשָׁרֵי נִיהֲלֵיהּ, כְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה.

a12.he: טְבָלִים — הֲוָה מַתְקֵינְנָא לְהוּ וְאָכֵלְנָא לְהוּ, יֵין נֶסֶךְ — עַל יְדֵי תַּעֲרוֹבֶת, וּכְרַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל.

a13.he: דִּתְנַן: יֵין נֶסֶךְ שֶׁנָּפַל לַבּוֹר — כּוּלּוֹ אָסוּר בַּהֲנָאָה. רַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל אוֹמֵר: יִמָּכֵר כּוּלּוֹ לְגוֹיִם, חוּץ מִדְּמֵי יֵין נֶסֶךְ שֶׁבּוֹ.

a15.he: מַתְנִי׳ עַל אֵלּוּ מוּמִין שׁוֹחֲטִין אֶת הַבְּכוֹר: נִפְגְּמָה אׇזְנוֹ מִן הַחַסְחוּס, אֲבָל לֹא הָעוֹר, נִסְדְּקָה אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁלֹּא חָסְרָה, נִיקְּבָה מְלֹא כַרְשִׁינָה, אוֹ שֶׁיָּבְשָׁה. אֵיזֶהוּ יְבֵשָׁה? כֹּל שֶׁתִּנָּקֵב וְאֵינָהּ מוֹצִיאָה טִיפַּת דָּם. רַבִּי יוֹסֵי בֶּן הַמְשׁוּלָּם אוֹמֵר: יְבֵשָׁה שֶׁתְּהֵא נִפְרֶכֶת.

a17.he: כְּתִיב נָמֵי ״כִּי יִהְיֶה בוֹ מוּם״, וְאֵימָא: ״כִּי יִהְיֶה בּוֹ מוּם״ — כָּלַל, ״פִּסֵּחַ אוֹ עִוֵּר״ — פָּרַט, כְּלָל וּפְרָט אֵין בַּכְּלָל אֶלָּא מָה שֶׁבַּפְּרָט; פִּסֵּחַ וְעִוֵּר — אִין, מִידֵּי אַחֲרִינָא — לָא!

a18.he: ״כֹּל מוּם רָע״ — חָזַר וְכָלַל, כְּלָל וּפְרָט וּכְלָל — אִי אַתָּה דָן אֶלָּא כְּעֵין הַפְּרָט; מָה הַפְּרָט מְפוֹרָשׁ — מוּמִין שֶׁבַּגָּלוּי וְאֵינָן חוֹזְרִין, אַף כֹּל מוּמִין שֶׁבַּגָּלוּי וְאֵינָן חוֹזְרִין.

a19.he: וְאֵימָא: מָה הַפְּרָט מְפוֹרָשׁ — מוּמִין שֶׁבַּגָּלוּי, וּבוֹטֵל מִמְּלַאכְתּוֹ, וְאֵינוֹ חוֹזֵר, אַף כֹּל — מוּמִין שֶׁבַּגָּלוּי, וּבוֹטֵל מִמְּלַאכְתּוֹ, וְאֵינוֹ חוֹזֵר. אַלְּמָה תְּנַן: נִפְגְּמָה אׇזְנוֹ מִן הַחַסְחוּס וְלֹא מִן הָעוֹר?

a20.he: כֹּל מוּם רָע רִיבּוּיָא הוּא, אִי הָכִי, מוּמִין שֶׁבַּסֵּתֶר נָמֵי? אַלְּמָה תְּנַן: חוּטִין הַחִיצוֹנוֹת שֶׁנִּפְגְּמוּ וְשֶׁנִּגְמְמוּ, וְהַפְּנִימִיּוֹת שֶׁנֶּעֶקְרוּ —

b1.he: נֶעְקְרוּ אִין, נִפְגְּמוּ וְנִגְמְמוּ לָא? בָּעֵינָא ״מוּם רָע״, וְלֵיכָּא! אִי הָכִי, מוּם עוֹבֵר נָמֵי! אַלְּמָה תְּנַן: וְלֹא מִן הָעוֹר?

b2.he: מוּם עוֹבֵר סְבָרָא הוּא, הַשְׁתָּא מִיפְרָק לָא פָּרְקִינַן עִלָּוֵיהּ, מִשְׁחָט שָׁחֲטִינַן עִלָּוֵיהּ? דְּתַנְיָא: ״וְאִם כׇּל בְּהֵמָה טְמֵאָה אֲשֶׁר לֹא יַקְרִיבוּ מִמֶּנָּה קׇרְבָּן לַה׳״ — בְּבַעֲלֵי מוּמִין הַכָּתוּב מְדַבֵּר.

b3.he: אַתָּה אוֹמֵר בְּבַעֲלֵי מוּמִין שֶׁנִּפְדּוּ הַכָּתוּב מְדַבֵּר, אוֹ אֵינוֹ אֶלָּא בִּבְהֵמָה טְמֵאָה מַמָּשׁ? כְּשֶׁהוּא אוֹמֵר ״וְאִם בִּבְהֵמָה הַטְּמֵאָה״, הֲרֵי בְּהֵמָה טְמֵאָה אָמוּר, הָא מָה אֲנִי מְקַיֵּים ״אֲשֶׁר לֹא יַקְרִיבוּ מִמֶּנָּה״? הֱוֵי אוֹמֵר: זֶה בַּעֲלֵי מוּמִין שֶׁנִּפְדּוּ.

b4.he: יָכוֹל יִפָּדוּ עַל מוּם עוֹבֵר? תַּלְמוּד לוֹמַר: ״אֲשֶׁר לֹא יַקְרִיבוּ מִמֶּנָּה קׇרְבָּן לַה׳״ — מִי שֶׁאֵינָהּ קְרֵיבָה כׇּל עִיקָּר, יָצְתָה זוֹ שֶׁאֵינָהּ קְרֵיבָה הַיּוֹם אֶלָּא לְמָחָר.

b5.he: אִיבָּעֵית אֵימָא: אִם כֵּן פִּסֵּחַ וְעִוֵּר לְמָה לִי?

b6.he: נִסְדְּקָה אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁלֹּא חָסְרָה. תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: הַסֶּדֶק — כׇּל שֶׁהוּא, הַפְּגִימָה — בֵּין בִּידֵי אָדָם בֵּין בִּידֵי שָׁמַיִם. מִכְּלָל דְּסֶדֶק בִּידֵי שָׁמַיִם לָא?

b7.he: אֶלָּא, סֶדֶק וּפְגִימָה — בֵּין בִּידֵי שָׁמַיִם בֵּין בִּידֵי אָדָם. וְכַמָּה שִׁיעוּר פְּגִימָה? כְּדֵי שֶׁתַּחְגּוֹר בָּהּ צִיפּוֹרֶן.

b8.he: נִקְּבָה מְלֹא וְכוּ׳. תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: כַּמָּה נְקִיבַת הָאוֹזֶן? מְלֹא כַרְשִׁינָה. רַבִּי יוֹסֵי בְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה אוֹמֵר: בְּכַעֲדָשָׁה. וְאֵיזוֹ הִיא יְבֵשָׁה? שֶׁאִם תִּינָּקֵב וְאֵינָהּ מוֹצִיאָה טִיפַּת דָּם. רַבִּי יוֹסֵי בֶּן הַמְשׁוּלָּם אוֹמֵר: יְבֵשָׁה כְּדֵי שֶׁתְּהֵא נִפְרֶכֶת.

b9.he: תָּנָא: קְרוֹבִין דִּבְרֵיהֶן לִהְיוֹת שָׁוִין. דִּבְרֵיהֶן דְּמַאן? אִילֵימָא דְּתַנָּא קַמָּא וְרַבִּי יוֹסֵי בֶּן הַמְשׁוּלָּם — טוּבָא אִיכָּא! אֶלָּא דְּתַנָּא קַמָּא וְרַבִּי יוֹסֵי בְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה.

b10.he: כַּעֲדָשָׁה — אִין, בְּצִיר מִכַּעֲדָשָׁה — לָא? וּרְמִינְהִי: ״מַרְצֵעַ״ — אֵין לִי אֶלָּא מַרְצֵעַ, מִנַּיִן לְרַבּוֹת הַסּוֹל, וְהַסִּירָה, וְהַמַּחַט, וְהַמַּקְדֵּחַ, וְהַמַּכְתֵּב?

b11.he: תַּלְמוּד לוֹמַר: ״וְלָקַחְתָּ״ — כׇּל דָּבָר שֶׁנִּלְקָח בַּיָּד, דִּבְרֵי רַבִּי יוֹסֵי בְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה. רַבִּי אוֹמֵר: ״מַרְצֵעַ״ — מָה מַרְצֵעַ מְיוּחָד שֶׁל מַתֶּכֶת, אַף כֹּל שֶׁל מַתֶּכֶת.

b12.he: וְקָתָנֵי סֵיפָא: אָמַר רַבִּי, יוּדָן בְּרִבִּי הָיָה דּוֹרֵשׁ: כְּשֶׁהֵן רוֹצְעִין, אֵין רוֹצְעִין אֶלָּא בַּמִּילָת.

b13.he: וַחֲכָמִים אוֹמְרִים: אֵין עֶבֶד עִבְרִי כֹּהֵן נִרְצָע, מִפְּנֵי שֶׁנַּעֲשָׂה בַּעַל מוּם. וְאִם תֹּאמַר: בַּמִּילָת הָיוּ רוֹצְעִין, הֵיאַךְ עֶבֶד כֹּהֵן נַעֲשֶׂה בַּעַל מוּם? הָא אֵין רוֹצְעִין אֶלָּא בְּגוֹבַהּ שֶׁל אוֹזֶן.

b14.he: אָמַר רַב חָנָא בַּר קַטִּינָא: לָא קַשְׁיָא — כָּאן לִשְׁחוֹט, כָּאן לִפְסוֹל.

b15.he: מַאי כַּרְשִׁינָה? אָמַר רַב שֵׁרֵבְיָא: הִינְדָּא.

b16.he: בְּעָא מִינֵּיהּ רַב הוֹשַׁעְיָא מֵרַב הוּנָא רַבָּה: כַּרְשִׁינָה הַנִּכְנֶסֶת וְיוֹצְאָה, אוֹ כַרְשִׁינָה הָעוֹמֶדֶת? אָמַר לוֹ: זוֹ לֹא שָׁמַעְתִּי, כַּיּוֹצֵא בָּהּ שָׁמַעְתִּי.

b17.he: דִּתְנַן: הַשִּׁדְרָה וְהַגּוּלְגּוֹלֶת שֶׁחָסְרוּ, כַּמָּה חֶסְרוֹן בַּשִּׁדְרָה וְלֹא יְהֵא מְטַמֵּא בְּאֹהֶל? בֵּית שַׁמַּאי אוֹמְרִים: שְׁתֵּי חוּלְיוֹת, וּבֵית הִלֵּל אוֹמְרִים: חוּלְיָא אַחַת. וּבַגּוּלְגּוֹלֶת, בֵּית שַׁמַּאי אוֹמְרִים: כִּמְלֹא מַקְדֵּחַ, וּבֵית הִלֵּל אוֹמְרִים: כְּדֵי שֶׁיִּנָּטֵל מִן הַחַי וְיָמוּת.

b18.he: וְיָתֵיב רַב חִסְדָּא וְקָמִיבַּעְיָא לֵיהּ: ״כְּדֵי שֶׁיִּנָּטֵל מִן הַחַי״ — וְכַמָּה? אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב תַּחְלִיפָא בַּר אֲבוּדִימִי: הָכִי אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל — כְּסֶלַע.

b19.he: וְאִיתְּמַר: רַב סָפְרָא אָמַר: שְׁמַעְתְּתָא אֲמַר לֵיהּ, וְרַב שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר יְהוּדָה אָמַר: מַתְנִיתָא אֲמַר לֵיהּ, וְסִימָנָיךְ: תָּנֵי רַב שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר יְהוּדָה.

b20.he: וַאֲמַר לֵיהּ: אִם כֵּן, עָשִׂיתָה דִּבְרֵי בֵּית שַׁמַּאי וְדִבְרֵי בֵּית הִלֵּל אֶחָד! דִּתְנַן: מָאוֹר שֶׁלֹּא נַעֲשָׂה בִּידֵי אָדָם, שִׁיעוּרוֹ מְלֹא אֶגְרוֹף גָּדוֹל, וְזֶהוּ אֶגְרוֹפוֹ שֶׁל בֶּן אֲבַטִּיחַ. אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹסֵי: וְיֶשְׁנוֹ כְּרֹאשׁ גָּדוֹל שֶׁל אָדָם.

b21.he: נַעֲשָׂה בִּידֵי אָדָם, שִׁיעֲרוּהוּ כִּמְלֹא מַקְדֵּחַ גָּדוֹל שֶׁל לִשְׁכָּה, שֶׁהוּא כְּפוּנְדְּיוֹן (שֶׁל) הָאִיטַלְקִי, וּכְסֶלַע נִירוֹנִית, וְיֶשְׁנוֹ

messages.text: Continued from 36b: Rav Ḥiyya bar Amram said that three laymen may permit a firstborn where there is no expert, and three may dissolve a vow where there is no Sage. The Gemara is explaining whom each ruling excludes.
is to the exclusion of the opinion of Rabbi Yosei in the mishna, who prohibits any number of laymen to deem a firstborn animal permitted.
messages.lead: …The ruling that a group of three laymen may permit a blemished firstborn in a place where there is no expert

notes.he: דמתני':
notes.en: To exclude Rabbi Yosei: of our mishna.

messages.text: The ruling that a group of three laymen may dissolve a vow in a place where there is no Sage is to the exclusion of the opinion of Rabbi Yehuda, as it is taught in a baraita:

notes.he: הא יש חכם הוא לבדו מתירו:
notes.en: In a place where there is no Sage: but where there is a Sage, he alone releases it.

notes.he: לישנא דקרא נקט אבל גבי חכם שייך לשון התרה וכן בהמוכר את הספינה (ב"ב דף עד.) גבי בת קול דקאמר ועכשיו שנשבעתי מי מפר לי:
notes.en: They dissolve [mefirin] the vow: he used the language of the verse [hafara]; but for a Sage the term hattara [release] applies. And so too in chapter HaMokher et HaSefina (Bava Batra 74a), concerning the Divine Voice, it says: “And now that I have sworn, who will annul [mefer] it for Me?”

notes.he: לאפוקי מדר' יהודה דלא בעינן אחד מהם חכם:
notes.en: To exclude Rabbi Yehuda: [for here] we do not require one of them to be a Sage.

messages.text: Dissolution of vows requires a court of three.
This is the halakha only if at least one of them is a Sage. If no Sage is available, laymen may not dissolve a vow.

Rav Ḥiyya bar Amram stated above that a group of three may dissolve a vow in a place where there is no Sage. This indicates that if there is a Sage, he alone may dissolve a vow. Who, for example, is considered such a Sage?

notes.he: הוי אותו חכם:
notes.en: Who, for example: would that Sage be?

messages.text: For example, one such as me.
messages.quote: Who, for example, is considered such a Sage?

messages.text: The baraita further stated that Rabbi Yehuda says: At least one of the three laymen must be a Sage. Should one conclude by inference that those other two members can be anyone, even complete ignoramuses?
messages.quote: only if at least one of them is a Sage

notes.he: בתמיה. כלומר אפי' עמי הארץ השנים ועמי הארץ היאך ראויין להצטרף:
notes.en: By inference, those two may be anyone?: [This is said] in astonishment. That is, even if the two are amei ha’aretz; and how are amei ha’aretz fit to join [the court]?

messages.text: Each member of the group must be one to whom the halakhot of vows is explained and he is able to comprehend them.

notes.he: טעמי הלכות נדרים וסברי ואותו חכם ילמד את השנים:
notes.en: Who are made to understand: the reasons of the halakhot of vows, and they understand; and that Sage will teach the two.

notes.dh: רבי יהודה אומר אחד מהם חכם מכלל דהנך כל דהו אמר רבינא דמסברי להו וסברי
notes.he: כ"כ ברוב הספרים ויש ספרים דגרסי כגון מאן אמר רב נחמן כגון אנא משמע מתוך לשון הקונט' שכך גריס וקשה היכי פריך עלה מכלל דהנך כל דהו אימא לא אלא שפחותים מדרב נחמן וא"ת לאידך גירסא נמי מנא ליה כל דהו דלמא מכלל דהנך פחותים ממומחה אבל כל דהו לא וי"ל דפשיטא ליה דחכם דר' יהודה לאו כחכם דלעיל דאיירי במומחה דאפי' רבי יהודה מודה דיחיד מומחה מתיר את הנדר וכאן דלא איירי במומחה מה שיעור נותן לאינך ומיהו קשה דא"כ מנא ליה דאתי לאפוקי מדרבי יהודה כיון דרבי יהודה לא איירי במומחה דלמא רבי חייא בר אבא מודה דבעינן אחד מהם כחכם דר' יהודה ודוחק לומר דג' מפירין את הנדר משמע ליה שלשתן שוין:
notes.en: “Rabbi Yehuda says: One of them is a Sage. By inference, those [others] are anyone? Ravina said: Who are made to understand and do understand”: so it is written in most books. And some books read: “Who, for example? Rav Naḥman said: For example, me,” and it appears from the language of the Kuntres [Rashi] that he read so. But it is difficult: how, then, does it object, “By inference, those [others] are anyone”? Say no; rather, [they need only be] less than Rav Naḥman! And if you ask: according to the other reading too, from where does it know [that they may be] anyone? Perhaps by inference those [others] are less than an expert, but not just anyone! One can answer: it is obvious to it that Rabbi Yehuda’s Sage is not like the Sage mentioned above, which refers to an expert, for even Rabbi Yehuda agrees that a single expert releases a vow; and here, since he is not speaking of an expert, what standard does he set for the others? But it is still difficult: if so, from where does it know that [the ruling of three] comes to exclude Rabbi Yehuda? Since Rabbi Yehuda is not speaking of an expert, perhaps Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba [so Tosafot’s text; the daf reads Rav Ḥiyya bar Amram] agrees that we require one of them to be like Rabbi Yehuda’s Sage. And it is forced to say that “three dissolve a vow” implies to it that all three are equal.

notes.he: דמסברי להו וסברי דלא ליהוו עמי הארץ גמורין:
notes.en: Who are made to understand and do understand: so that they are not complete amei ha’aretz.

messages.text: § The mishna teaches that Rabbi Yosei says: Even if there is a court of twenty-three Sages there, it may be slaughtered only on the basis of the ruling of an expert.
The halakha is not in accordance with the opinion of Rabbi Yosei.
This is obvious, as there is a principle that in a dispute between an individual Sage and many Sages, the halakha is in accordance with the opinion of the many Sages.
messages.quote: The halakha is not in accordance with the opinion of Rabbi Yosei

messages.text: Rav’s statement is necessary, lest you say that Rabbi Yosei is an exception to the principle, as his reasoning [nimmuko] is with him, i.e., his logic is sound. Rav Ḥananel therefore teaches us that this is not so, and the halakha does not follow his opinion.

notes.he: הא קיימא לן במסכת גיטין (דף סז.) רבי יוסי נימוקו עמו ותיהוי הלכתא כוותיה:
notes.en: Lest you say: we hold in tractate Gittin (67a) that Rabbi Yosei, “his reasoning is with him,” so let the halakha be in accordance with him.

notes.he: טעמו. שהיה מביא טעם לדבריו כל שעה:
notes.en: Nimmuko: his reason. For he would bring a reason for his statements at all times.

messages.text: Earlier (36b), the Gemara cited a ruling, which was issued either by Rav or Shmuel, that three regular Jews may deem a firstborn animal permitted in a place where there is no expert, in contrast to the opinion of Rabbi Yosei. Resolve that dilemma from this statement in the name of Rav, that the halakha is not in accordance with the opinion of Rabbi Yosei.
messages.quote: not in accordance with the opinion of Rabbi Yosei

notes.he: דאמר רב חננאל משמיה דרב אין הלכה כר' יוסי תפשוט דהך קמייתא דאמר רב יהודה לעיל ספק משמיה דרב ספק משמיה דשמואל ג' מתירין את הבכור תפשוט משמיה דשמואל איתמר דאי משמיה דרב תרתי למה ליה למימר לרב תרתי זימני דשלשה מתירין את הבכור ואין הלכה כר' יוסי:
notes.en: Resolve from this: from what Rav Ḥananel said in the name of Rav, “The halakha is not in accordance with Rabbi Yosei,” resolve that the earlier statement, which Rav Yehuda said above, uncertain whether in the name of Rav or in the name of Shmuel, “Three permit the firstborn,” was stated in the name of Shmuel. For if it were in the name of Rav, why would Rav need to say twice that three permit the firstborn and that the halakha is not in accordance with Rabbi Yosei?

messages.text: It can be inferred from here that that first, uncertain ruling was stated in the name of Shmuel. As, if it was stated in the name of Rav, why do I need two identical rulings?

This is insufficient proof, as it is possible that Rav did not issue two identical rulings. Rather, one ruling was stated from the other, by inference. Rav issued only one of these statements explicitly; the other was reported by his students in his name based on an inference from what he had said.

notes.he: תיפשוט מהא דמדהא איתמר משמיה דרב ש"מ דהך קמייתא דאמרינן ספק משמיה דרב ספק משמי' דשמואל דודאי דשמואל היא דאי ההיא נמי משמיה דרב והכא נמי אמר רב הלכה כר' יוסי אלא דאפי' ג' בני כנסת מתירין היינו קמייתא תרי זימני למה לי למימר. לא ודאי לא איתמר אלא חדא משמיה דרב ואידך מכללא. מדוקיא דההיא איתמר ואליבא דרב:
notes.en: Resolve from this: since this was stated in the name of Rav, learn from it that the earlier one, of which we said it was uncertain whether in the name of Rav or in the name of Shmuel, is certainly Shmuel’s. For if that one too were in the name of Rav, and here too Rav said the halakha is [not] in accordance with Rabbi Yosei [the printed text lacks “not”], but that even three members of the synagogue permit, that is the same as the earlier one; why would he need to say it twice? No: certainly only one was stated in the name of Rav, and the other by inference; it was stated by inference from that one, according to Rav.

messages.text: Mishna

In the case of one who slaughters a firstborn animal and sells its meat, and it was discovered that he did not initially show it to one of the Sages, the halakha is that it was actually prohibited to derive any benefit from the meat.

notes.he: ומכר מבשרו:
notes.en: Mishna. One who slaughters the firstborn: and sold some of its meat.

notes.he: לחכם:
notes.en: And it became known that he did not show it: to a Sage.

messages.text: In that case, what the buyers ate, they ate, and the Sages penalized the seller in that he must return the money to them, which they paid for the meat that they ate.

notes.he: הלוקחים אכלו:
notes.en: What they ate: the buyers ate.

notes.he: משום קנס דאיסור ספק הוי:
notes.en: And he returns the money to them: as a penalty, since it was a doubtful prohibition.

notes.he: דקנסוהו רבנן:
notes.en: And he returns the money to them: for the Rabbis penalized him.

messages.text: And with regard to that which they did not eat, that meat must be buried, and he must return the money that they paid for the meat that they did not eat.

notes.he: דבכור תם אסור בהנאה:
notes.en: The meat must be buried: for an unblemished firstborn is prohibited for benefit.

messages.text: And likewise, in the case of one who slaughters a cow and sells it, and it was discovered that it is a tereifa, what the buyers ate, they ate, and what they did not eat, they must return the meat to the seller, who may sell it to a gentile or feed it to the dogs, and he must return the money to the buyers.

notes.he: הן יחזירו לו את הבשר שמותר בהנאתו שרשאי למוכרו לעובד כוכבים:
notes.en: They return the meat to him: for it is permitted for benefit, since he may sell it to a gentile.

messages.text: If the buyers sold it to gentiles or cast it to the dogs, they pay the seller the value of a tereifa, which is less than the value of kosher meat, and the seller refunds the balance to the buyers.

notes.he: הלוקחים לעובדי כוכבים הואיל ולא גרם להו איסורא ישלמו לו דמי בשר טריפה בזול והוא יחזיר להם המותר:
notes.en: They sold it: the buyers [sold it] to gentiles. Since he did not cause them [to eat] a prohibition, they pay him the price of tereifa meat, which is cheap, and he returns the remainder to them.

notes.he: מכרוהו הלוקחין את הבשר לעובד כוכבים ביוקר או הטילוהו לכלבים ועדיין לא נתנו הדמים ישלמו לו דמי טרפה שהיא בזול ולא ישלמו לו כל הדמים שנטלו ממנה לפי שהוא מכר טרפה מדעתו:
notes.en: The buyers sold the meat to a gentile at a high price, or cast it to the dogs, and have not yet paid the money: they pay him the value of a tereifa, which is cheap, and do not pay him all the money they received for it, because he sold a tereifa of his own accord.

messages.text: Gemara

In a case where one sells meat to another and it was discovered that it is the meat of a firstborn animal, which was not deemed permitted for consumption by an expert, or if one sells produce to another and it was discovered that it is untithed produce, or if one sells wine to another and it turns out that it is wine that was used for a libation in idol worship, the halakha is that what the purchasers ate, they ate, and the seller reimburses them all their money.

If he sold them items from which one is generally repulsed, he must reimburse them all their money, as they are presumed to not have derived benefit from the consumption of such items. But if he sold them items from which one is not generally repulsed, he deducts for them the value of the benefit from those items and reimburses them the balance.

notes.he: מואסת כמו ואקוץ בם (ויקרא כ):
notes.en: Gemara. Katza: is repulsed, as in “and I abhorred [va’akutz] them” (Leviticus 20[:23]).

notes.he: דכל מה שאכלו אינו נהנה להם משעה שנודע להם:
notes.en: He returns to them all the money: for nothing of what they ate is of benefit to them, from the moment it became known to them.

notes.he: והוא יטול קצת בתמיה:
notes.en: He deducts: and so he takes a little [of the money]? [This is said] in astonishment.

notes.he: ינכה להם מן הדמים כנגד מה שאכלו והשאר יחזיר:
notes.en: He deducts from the money for them, corresponding to what they ate, and returns the rest.

messages.text: And the following are items from which one is generally repulsed: Carcasses and tereifot, repugnant creatures, and creeping animals. And the following are items from which one is generally not repulsed: Firstborn animals, untithed produce, and wine used for a libation in idol worship.

notes.he: אע"ג דבפ' ג' דהוריות (דף יא.) קאמר דסתמו הוי אפיקורוס ביין נסך כמו בנבילות מ"מ לא חשיב נפש קצה בו ועוד דהכא מסקינן על ידי תערובות:
notes.en: And libation wine: even though in the third chapter of Horayot (11a) it says that one who [eats] it ordinarily is a heretic with regard to libation wine, as with carcasses, nevertheless it is not counted as something one is repulsed by. And furthermore, here we conclude [that it is] by way of a mixture.

messages.text: Why does the seller deduct the value of the meat of a firstborn animal eaten by the purchaser and reimburse him the difference? Let the purchaser say to the seller: What loss have I caused you by eating the meat? Had you not sold it to me, you would have had no rights to partake of it, as this is an unblemished firstborn animal from which deriving benefit is prohibited.

notes.he: ישראל לכהן שמכר מה אפסדתך הלא אם היה הבשר בידך היה טעון קבורה שהרי תם שחטתו:
notes.en: And let him say to him: the Israelite to the priest who sold [it]: What loss did I cause you? Had the meat been in your hand, it would have required burial, since you slaughtered it unblemished.

messages.text: No, this ruling is necessary in a case where he sold him a cut of meat from an area on the animal that contained a blemish, but the seller had not yet brought the animal to be examined and deemed permitted by a Sage. In that instance, the seller can say to the purchaser: Had you not eaten the meat, I would have shown the animal to a Sage and he would have deemed it permitted to me.

notes.he: כהן השוחט מקום המום לישראל:
notes.en: For example, where he sold him: the priest who slaughtered [it sold] the place of the blemish to the Israelite.

notes.he: כהן אם היה בידי הוה מחזינא ליה כמו שהוא שחוט:
notes.en: For he says to him: the priest [says]: Had it been in my hand, I would have shown it [to a Sage] as it is, slaughtered.

notes.he: בכור אמאי ינכה לו מן הדמים לימא ליה הלוקח מאי אפסידתך דאכלתיה והא אי אהדרתיה ניהלך לא הוי תקנה אלא יקבר. כגון דזבין ההוא אבר דהוה ביה מומא ואכליה ומשום הכי ינכה ליה מן הדמים:
notes.en: A firstborn: why should he deduct from the money? Let the buyer say to him: What loss did I cause you by eating it? For had I returned it to you, there would be no remedy; it would be buried. [The answer:] for example, where he sold that limb that had a blemish, and he ate it; and therefore he deducts from the money.

notes.he: דאמר ליה אי לאו דאכלתיה הוה מחזינא ליה לחכם ושרי לי ניהליה:
notes.en: For he says to him: Had you not eaten it, I would have shown it to a Sage and he would have permitted it to me.

messages.text: This is in accordance with the opinion of Rabbi Yehuda (28a), who permits a firstborn animal to be examined and deemed permitted even after it has been slaughtered.

notes.he: דאמרינן בפרק עד כמה (לעיל בכורות כח.) השוחט את הבכור ואחר כך הראה את מומו רבי יהודה מתיר:
notes.en: In accordance with Rabbi Yehuda: as we say in chapter Ad Kama (above, Bekhorot 28a): One who slaughters the firstborn and afterward shows its blemish, Rabbi Yehuda permits.

notes.he: דמתיר לראות מום לאחר שחיטה כדאמרינן בפרקין דלעילא:
notes.en: In accordance with Rabbi Yehuda: who permits examining a blemish after slaughter, as we said in the chapter above.

messages.text: With regard to untithed produce, although one could claim that the purchaser did not cause a loss to the seller, as untithed produce is prohibited for consumption, the seller can say to the purchaser: Had you not eaten my produce, I would have remedied it, i.e., separated its tithes, and eaten it.

notes.he: אמאי יטול קצת לימא ליה מוכר ללוקח אי לאו דאכלתנהו הוה מתקננא להו:
notes.en: Untithed produce: why does he take a little? [Because] the seller can say to the buyer: Had you not eaten them, I would have remedied them.

messages.text: Similarly, with regard to wine used for a libation in idol worship, which is also prohibited to be consumed, this is referring to a seller who sold it in a mixture of permitted wine. In this case, had the purchaser not consumed the wine mixture, the seller could have derived benefit from it, in accordance with the opinion of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.

notes.he: אמאי יטול קצת. [ומשני] כגון דלא זבין ליה יין נסך גופיה אלא עירבו עם יין כשר ומכרן לימא ליה אי הדרתיה ניהלי הוה מזביננא ליה לעובדי כוכבים חוץ מדמי יין נסך שבו:
notes.en: Libation wine: why does he take a little? [And it answers:] for example, where he did not sell him the libation wine itself, but mixed it with kosher wine and sold them. He can say to him: Had you returned it to me, I would have sold it to gentiles, except for the value of the libation wine in it.

notes.he: מצי א"ל אי לאו דאכלת מתקנינא להו הלכך ינכה. ויין נסך שאינו נסך גרידא אלא ע"י תערובת נתנסך וזבני ניהליה ואי הוה מהדר ליה הוה מותר בהנאתו כדרשב"ג דתנן וכו' הלכך ינכה:
notes.en: Untithed produce: he can say to him: Had you not eaten [it], I would have remedied them; therefore he deducts. And libation wine: [wine] that is not libation wine alone, but became libation wine through a mixture, and he sold it to him; had he returned it to him, it would have been permitted for benefit, in accordance with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, as we learned, etc. Therefore he deducts.

messages.text: In the case of wine used for a libation in idol worship that fell into a wine cistern, it is prohibited to derive benefit from all the wine in the cistern, even if the volume of the wine used for a libation was small in comparison to the volume of the rest of the wine in the cistern.
All of the wine in the cistern may be sold to a gentile, and the money paid for it is permitted, except for the value of the wine used for a libation that is in it.

notes.he: סליק פירקא
notes.en: The chapter is concluded.

messages.text: הדרן עלך כל פסולי המוקדשין · Hadran alakh Kol Pesulei HaMukdashin: we will return to you, chapter 5, “All Disqualified Consecrated Animals.”
Chapter 6 · על אלו מומין · Al Elu Mumin: the blemishes for which a firstborn may be slaughtered outside the Temple, beginning with the ear.
Mishna
For these blemishes, one may slaughter the firstborn animal outside the Temple: If the firstborn’s ear was damaged and lacking from the cartilage [haḥasḥus], but not if the skin was damaged;

notes.he: מתני' על אלו מומין:
notes.en: Mishna. For these blemishes: [Rashi gives only the opening words of the new chapter.]

notes.he: תנוך האוזן שקורין טנדרי"ן:
notes.en: The ḥasḥus: the cartilage [tenukh] of the ear, which is called (Rashi adds an Old French gloss).

notes.he: דהדר בריא ולא הוי מומא. והאי עור היינו אליה רכה של אוזן:
notes.en: But not from the skin: for it becomes healthy again and is not a blemish. And this “skin” is the soft lobe of the ear.

notes.he: לשון חנוך הוא כמו ראשי כנפים והחסחין בפרק כיצד צולין (פסחים פד.) ובדל האוזן מתרגם חסחוס דאודנא (עמוס ג):
notes.en: Mishna. From the ḥasḥus: it means cartilage [tenukh], as in “the tips of the wings and the ḥasḥot” in chapter Keitzad Tzolin (Pesaḥim 84a); and “a piece of an ear” (Amos 3[:12]) is rendered [in the Aramaic translation] “ḥasḥus de’udna.”

notes.he: הסחוס שלועזים טנדרוס:
notes.en: For these blemishes. The ḥasḥus: which is called in the vernacular (Rabbeinu Gershom adds an Old French gloss).

messages.text: and likewise, if the ear was split, although it is not lacking;

notes.he: פגימה אינה בלא חסרון אבל סדק משמע נמי בלא חסרון:
notes.en: [On the wording:] Damage [pegima] does not occur without something missing, but “split” implies even without something missing.

messages.text: or if the ear was pierced with a hole the size of a bitter vetch, which is a type of legume;

notes.he: כמלא הכנסת גרגר של כרשינין:
notes.en: The size of a karshina: as much as [allows] the insertion of a karshina seed.

messages.text: or if it was an ear that is desiccated. What is a desiccated ear that is considered a blemish? It is any ear that if it is pierced it does not discharge a drop of blood.
Desiccated means that the ear is so dry that it will crumble if one touches it.

notes.he: כשממשמשין בה:
notes.en: Crumbles: when one touches it.

messages.text: Gemara

With regard to the blemishes mentioned in this mishna and in the subsequent mishnayot: Why is it permitted to slaughter and eat a firstborn that sustained these blemishes? Only a lame animal and a blind animal are written in the verse that discusses this halakha. That verse states: “And if there be any blemish therein, lameness, or blindness, any ill blemish whatsoever, you shall not sacrifice it to the Lord your God. You shall eat it within your gates.”

verse.he: וְכִי־יִהְיֶה בוֹ מוּם פִּסֵּחַ אוֹ עִוֵּר כֹּל מוּם רָע לֹא תִזְבָּחֶנּוּ לַיהֹוָה אֱלֹהֶיךָ׃ בִּשְׁעָרֶיךָ תֹּאכְלֶנּוּ הַטָּמֵא וְהַטָּהוֹר יַחְדָּו כַּצְּבִי וְכָאַיָּל׃
verse.en: But if it has a defect, lameness or blindness, any serious defect, you shall not sacrifice it to the ETERNAL your God. Eat it in your settlements, the impure among you no less than the pure, just like the gazelle and the deer.

notes.he: שישחוט בכור עליהן ומידי אחרינא לא דכתיב וכי יהיה בו מום פסח ועור וסמיך ליה בשעריך תאכלנו דהיינו בלא הקרבה:
notes.en: Gemara. But why? Lame and blind are written: [as the blemishes] for which one may slaughter a firstborn, and not anything else, as it is written: “And if there be any blemish therein, lame or blind,” and adjacent to it: “You shall eat it within your gates,” that is, without sacrifice.

notes.he: אמאי נשחטו על אלו מומין:
notes.en: Why are they slaughtered for these blemishes?

notes.he: בלבד כתיבי:
notes.en: Lame and blind: alone are written.

messages.text: It is also written in the beginning of the verse: “If there be any blemish therein,” which indicates that other blemishes are also included.

notes.dh: ומשני כתיב נמי כי יהיה בו מום
notes.he: דמשמע נמי מומין אחריני:
notes.en: And it answers: “If there be any blemish therein” is also written: which implies other blemishes as well.

notes.he: כתיב נמי כי יהיה בו מום סתם ריבה את אלו:
notes.en: “If there be any blemish therein” is also written, unspecified: it included these.

messages.text: But why not say that the phrase “if there be any blemish therein” is a generalization, while “lameness, or blindness” is a detail. According to the principles of midrashic exegesis, if a generalization and a detail are mentioned, the generalization includes only that which is specified in the detail. Therefore, it should be concluded that in the event of lameness and blindness, yes, one may slaughter the firstborn, but in the event of another matter, one may not slaughter it.

By subsequently stating: “Any ill blemish,” it then generalized again. Consequently, it is a generalization and a detail and a generalization, represented in the phrases “any blemish,” “lameness or blindness,” and “any ill blemish,” and according to the principles of midrashic exegesis, you may deduce that the verse is referring only to items similar to the detail.

Just as the items mentioned in the detail, i.e., in the phrase “lameness or blindness,” are clearly defined as blemishes that are exposed and do not regenerate, so too, all blemishes that are exposed and do not regenerate are considered blemishes with regard to a firstborn.

notes.dh: מה הפרט מפורש מומין שבגלוי ואינן חוזרין
notes.he: כה"ג דרשינן בפ"ק דקדושין (דף כד:) גבי שן ועין וא"ת ומ"ט לא הוי הכא מומא כשנפלה שינו כיון דחשיב מום שבגלוי ואינו חוזר דלקמן בפרק מומין אלו (בכורות דף מד.) לא פסלינן ניטלו שיניו גבי אדם אלא משום מראית העין דאינו שוה בזרעו של אהרן מכלל דבבהמה כשר ואפי' גבי אדם לא מיפסל בשן אחד ודוקא בחוטין החיצונות שנפגמו ושנגממו ובפנימיות שנעקרו ינציב"ש בלע"ז כדפירש בקונטרס קאמר בסמוך גבי בהמה דהוי מום אבל ניטלו שינים לא וי"ל דשאני גבי עבד דגלי קרא אבל הכא שכך דרך שהשינים נופלות מחמת זקנה לא הוי כעין פסח ועור ומיהו צריך טעם אחר דה"נ עיניו מחמת זקנה וא"ת מאי שנא דהכהו על אזנו וחרשו חשיב מום התם ועבד יוצא לחירות דהוי מום שבגלוי ואינו חוזר ולקמן בפרק אלו מומין (בכורות דף מה:) תנן חרש שוטה (וקטן) פסולין באדם וכשרין בבהמה באדם לא מיפסלי אלא משום דאינו שוה בזרעו של אהרן כדמפרש לקמן בין חרש בידי אדם לחרש בידי שמים וי"ל דגבי עבד גלי רחמנא דבדבר קל חשיב מום לצאת בו לחירות שמשתחרר בשינו:
notes.en: In brief: Tosafot note that the same exposition, “exposed blemishes that do not return,” is used in the first chapter of Kiddushin (24b) for the tooth and eye that free a slave. They ask: why, then, is a fallen tooth not a blemish in an animal, since it is exposed and does not grow back? [For below, in chapter Mumin Elu (Bekhorot 44a), a priest whose teeth were removed is disqualified only for appearance, since he is not equal among Aaron’s offspring, which implies that an animal is fit; and even a person is not disqualified for one tooth; and for an animal the Gemara here counts only damaged or scratched external gums and extracted internal ones, not lost teeth.] They answer that a slave is different, since the verse revealed it; but here, since teeth normally fall out with age, it is not like lameness and blindness. They note that another reason is still needed, since the eyes too [fail] with age. They ask further: why does striking a slave on the ear and deafening him count there as an exposed blemish that does not return, so that he goes free, while in chapter Elu Mumin (Bekhorot 45b) we learned that a deaf-mute and an imbecile are disqualified in a person and fit in an animal, and in a person only because he is not equal among Aaron’s offspring? They answer that for a slave the Merciful One revealed that even a slight thing counts as a blemish to go free, for he goes free for his tooth. Open on Sefaria for the full text.

messages.text: But say instead that just as the items mentioned in the detail, i.e., in the phrase “lameness or blindness,” are clearly defined as blemishes that are exposed and that cause an animal to desist from its normal labor, and they are blemishes that do not regenerate, so too, all blemishes that are exposed and that cause an animal to desist from its labor and do not regenerate are included in this halakha.

notes.he: כגון פסח בטל מהילוך ועור בטל מראייה:
notes.en: And it also desists from its labor: for example, a lame animal is kept from walking and a blind one from seeing.

notes.he: ובטל ממלאכתו פסח ועור שאינו ראוי למלאכה:
notes.en: And it desists from its labor: lame and blind, which are not fit for labor.

messages.text: If so, a blemish that does not fit these criteria would not render the firstborn permitted to be slaughtered. Why then did we learn in the mishna that if the firstborn’s ear was damaged and lacking from the cartilage, but not if it is lacking from the skin, it is considered a blemish, despite the fact that this does not cause the animal to desist from its labor?
messages.quote: ear was damaged and lacking from the cartilage

notes.he: הוי מום הא אינה בטילה משמיעה:
notes.en: Why then did we learn: “its ear was damaged” is a blemish? But it is not kept from hearing!

notes.he: אלמה תנן נפגם אזנו דמשום הכי אינו בטל וקא הוי מום:
notes.en: Why then did we learn: “its ear was damaged”? For on that account it does not desist [from labor], and yet it is a blemish.

messages.text: The word “any” in “any ill blemish” is an amplification, and it includes even blemishes that are different from those defined by the detail.

notes.he: דכתיב כל ולא דרשינן ליה בכלל ופרט:
notes.en: It is an amplification: for “any” [kol] is written, and we do not expound it by [the rule of] generalization and detail.

notes.he: כל מום רע ריבויא הוא ומרבי הני:
notes.en: “Any ill blemish” is an amplification: and it includes these.

messages.text: If so, blemishes that are hidden should also be included. Why then did we learn in the mishna (39a) that animals with external gums that were damaged and lacking or that were scratched [veshenigmemu] and likewise animals with internal gums that were entirely extracted are considered blemished?

notes.he: דריבויא הוא מומין שבסתר נשחוט נמי עלייהו:
notes.en: If so: that it is an amplification, let one slaughter for hidden blemishes as well.

notes.he: יינצב"ש:
notes.en: Gums: (Rashi adds an Old French gloss).

notes.he: שבאמצע הפה:
notes.en: External: those in the middle of the mouth.

notes.he: שחסרו מעט:
notes.en: That were damaged: that were slightly lacking.

notes.he: שנחתכו בסכין ברוחבו ולא חיסרו אלא כעין סדק:
notes.en: That were scratched [shenigmemu]: that were cut across their width with a knife, and nothing was lacking, but [it is] like a split.

notes.he: מונשליר"ש:
notes.en: The internal: (Rashi adds an Old French gloss).

notes.he: חניכים החיצוניות הוי מום כי נגממו משום דלא הוי בסתר דמיתחזי כדאכיל:
notes.en: Gums: the external gums are a blemish when they are scratched, because it is not hidden, since it is visible when it eats.

messages.text: It can be inferred that if the internal gums were extracted then yes, one may slaughter the firstborn, but if they were merely damaged or they were scratched, one may not, since it is a hidden blemish.

notes.he: הוי מצי לאתויי מההיא דלקמן דקא חשיב בהדיא גבי ואלו שאין שוחטין עליהן לא במקדש ולא במדינה חוטין הפנימיות שנפגמו ונגממו אלא ניחא לאתויי מדיוקא דרישא דמוכח דאע"ג דבחיצוניות הוי מום שבגלוי בפנימיות לא הוי מום:
notes.en: Extracted, yes; damaged or scratched, no: it could have cited the case below, which explicitly lists among “these are the ones for which one does not slaughter, neither in the Temple nor in the country” internal gums that were damaged or scratched. But it preferred to cite the inference from the first clause, which shows that even though in the external [gums] it is an exposed blemish, in the internal ones it is not a blemish.

messages.text: I require that it be an “ill blemish,” which must be exposed and degrading, and a hidden blemish is not considered such an “ill blemish.”

notes.he: אלא בגלוי שמנוולו:
notes.en: [A hidden blemish] is not called an ill blemish: only an exposed one, which makes it unsightly [is called so].

notes.he: דמיתחזי מום רע וליכא כלומר היינו מיגוואי אי לא נעקרו ממש לא הוי מום רע דלא מיתחזי:
notes.en: I require: that an ill blemish be visible, and there is none. That is, these are internal; if they were not actually extracted, it is not an ill blemish, since it is not visible.

messages.text: If so, that all blemishes are included by the words: “Any ill blemish,” aside from hidden blemishes, a temporary blemish should also render it permitted for the firstborn to be slaughtered. Why then did we learn in the mishna: If the firstborn’s ear was damaged and lacking from the cartilage it may be slaughtered, but not if it is damaged and lacking from the skin, since it is a temporary blemish?
messages.quote: but not if the skin was damaged

notes.he: דכל מום ריבויא הוא:
notes.en: If so: that “any blemish” is an amplification.

notes.he: דמיתחזי ליהוי מום רע ולשחוט עליה אלמה תנן ולא מן העור כו':
notes.en: If so, a temporary blemish: which is visible, should count as an ill blemish, and one should slaughter for it. Why then did we learn: “and not from the skin,” etc.?

messages.text: A temporary blemish is not excluded by the exegesis but is based on logical reasoning: Now, if we do not even redeem an offering due to a temporary blemish, will we slaughter a firstborn outside the Temple, for which redemption is not performed, due to a temporary blemish?

notes.he: פסולי המוקדשין:
notes.en: Now, we do not redeem on account of it: [we do not redeem] disqualified consecrated animals [for a temporary blemish].

notes.he: בכור בחוץ:
notes.en: Will we slaughter on account of it: a firstborn outside [the Temple]?

notes.dh: השתא מיפרק לא פרקינן עילוי' כו'
notes.he: וא"ת להאי שנוייא קמא דנפיק מום עובר מק"ו פסח ועור מאי אהני ליה וי"ל דקסבר השתא דאי לא כתיב פסח ועור קמרבינן מכל מום רע מום עובר והוה אמינא דאתא לאפוקי מק"ו ולא ממעטינן נמי ממום רע מומין שבסתר:
notes.en: Now, we do not redeem on account of it, etc.: And if you ask: according to this first answer, that a temporary blemish is excluded by an a fortiori argument, what does “lame and blind” accomplish? One can answer: it holds now that if “lame and blind” were not written, we would include a temporary blemish from “any ill blemish,” and I would have said that it comes to exclude [the conclusion of] the a fortiori argument; and we would also not exclude hidden blemishes from “ill blemish.”

notes.he: דלא לשחוט עליה דהשתא מיפרק לא פרקינן על מום עובר מישחט כו'. ואי בעית אימא א"כ הוא דנשחט על מום עובר פסח ועור מה אהני למכתב אלא ש"מ דאינו נשחט אלא על מום קבוע דומיא דפסח ועור:
notes.en: A temporary blemish is logical reasoning: that one should not slaughter for it; for now that we do not redeem for a temporary blemish, will we slaughter, etc.? And if you wish, say: if so, that one may slaughter for a temporary blemish, what does it help to write “lame and blind”? Rather, learn from it that one slaughters only for a permanent blemish, like lame and blind.

messages.text: The source for this assertion that an offering is not redeemed because of a temporary blemish: As it is taught in a baraita:
“And if it be any impure animal, of which they may not bring an offering to the Lord.” The verse is speaking of ritually pure animals with blemishes.

verse.he: וְאִם כׇּל־בְּהֵמָה טְמֵאָה אֲשֶׁר לֹא־יַקְרִיבוּ מִמֶּנָּה קׇרְבָּן לַיהֹוָה וְהֶעֱמִיד אֶת־הַבְּהֵמָה לִפְנֵי הַכֹּהֵן׃
verse.en: If [the vow concerns] any impure animal that may not be brought as an offering to GOD, the animal shall be presented before the priest,

messages.text: Do you say that the verse is speaking of animals with blemishes that were redeemed, or is it referring only to an actual impure animal, such as a donkey or a horse that was consecrated; but with regard to a kosher animal, perhaps its consecrated status cannot be removed by redemption even if it was blemished?

When the verse states: “And if it be of an impure animal,” a non-kosher animal is mentioned. So how do I realize the meaning of: “Of which they may not bring an offering”? You must say that this is referring to blemished animals that were redeemed, indicating that redemption is permitted.

verse.he: וְאִם בַּבְּהֵמָה הַטְּמֵאָה וּפָדָה בְעֶרְכֶּךָ וְיָסַף חֲמִשִׁתוֹ עָלָיו וְאִם־לֹא יִגָּאֵל וְנִמְכַּר בְּעֶרְכֶּךָ׃
verse.en: But if it is of impure animals, it may be ransomed at its assessment, with one-fifth added; if it is not redeemed, it shall be sold at its assessment.

notes.he: פסוק אחר ואם בבהמה הטמאה ופדה בערכך:
notes.en: When it says: [in] another verse: “And if it be of an impure animal, then he shall redeem it according to your valuation” [Leviticus 27:27].

messages.text: One might have thought that offerings may be redeemed due to a temporary blemish that they sustained. Therefore, the verse states: “Of which they may not bring an offering to the Lord.” This teaches that an animal that is not sacrificed at all is redeemed, which excludes this animal that has a temporary blemish, which is not sacrificed today, but rather may be sacrificed tomorrow.

If you wish, say a different explanation as to why a temporary blemish is not included in the amplification of the verse: “Any ill blemish”: If so, that even a temporary blemish permits its slaughter, why do I need the verse to mention a lame animal and a blind animal? It would have sufficed to state: “Any ill blemish.” Rather, the verse excludes a temporary blemish that is unlike these two blemishes, which are permanent.

notes.he: דבעל מום עובר נמי נפדין פסח ועור מאי אהני ליה דמשמע מומין קבועין ולא עוברין:
notes.en: If so: that animals with a temporary blemish are also redeemed, what did “lame and blind” accomplish? For they imply permanent blemishes and not temporary ones.

messages.caption: How the Gemara narrows “any ill blemish”: each proposed rule, the mishna case that tests it, and the answer.

messages.text: § The mishna teaches: If the ear of the firstborn animal was split, although it is not lacking, one may slaughter the animal outside the Temple. With regard to this, the Sages taught in a baraita:
messages.quote: was split, although it is not lacking

messages.text: The split that permits the animal to be slaughtered is one of any size. With regard to the damage, whether it was done by the hand of a person or by the hand of God, it may be slaughtered.

Should it be derived by inference that with regard to a split, if it was caused by the hand of God it is not considered a blemish? That also should be considered an obvious blemish and render the animal permitted for slaughter.
messages.quote: the damage, whether it was done by the hand of a person or by the hand of God

notes.he: שנולד עמו:
notes.en: By the hand of Heaven: that it was born with it.

messages.text: Rather, the baraita should be interpreted as follows: The animal may be slaughtered for a split of any size, and with regard to a split and damage, whether it was done by the hand of God or by the hand of a person, the animal may be slaughtered.

And what is the measure of the damage that is considered a blemish? It must be large enough that a fingernail will be retained [shetaḥgor] on it, i.e., if one passes his fingernail over the ear of the animal it can enter the area of the damage.

notes.he: שתעכב בה צפורן אם בודקין כבדיקת סכין:
notes.en: Shetaḥgor: that a fingernail catches in it, if one checks [it] the way one checks a knife.

messages.text: § The mishna stated that if the ear of a firstborn animal was pierced with a hole the size of a bitter vetch, the animal is slaughtered because of it. With regard to this, the Sages taught in a baraita:
messages.quote: was pierced with a hole the size of a bitter vetch

messages.text: How large must the piercing of the ear be? It must be the size of a karshina.
Like the size of a lentil, which is slightly smaller.
And what is a desiccated ear that is considered a blemish? It is an ear that if it is pierced, it does not discharge a drop of blood.
Desiccated means that the ear is so dry that it will crumble if one touches it.
Their statements are close to being identical in practice.

The statements of whom are close to being identical? If we say that he is referring to the statements of the first tanna and Rabbi Yosei ben HaMeshullam with regard to a desiccated ear, there is a significant difference between these two opinions. One says it is determined by whether blood emerges, while the other holds it is based on whether it crumbles.
messages.quote: Their statements are close to being identical

messages.text: Rather, he is referring to the statement of the first tanna and the statement of Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Yehuda, as a karshina and a lentil are almost identical in size.

notes.he: דכרשינה אינה גדולה מעדשה אלא מעט:
notes.en: Rather, of the first tanna and Rabbi Yosei: for a karshina is only slightly larger than a lentil.

notes.he: אלא דת"ק ורבי יוסי בן (המשולם) [יהודה] בין כרשינה ועדשה איכא פורתא:
notes.en: Rather, of the first tanna and Rabbi Yosei son of (HaMeshullam) [Yehuda] [the text is corrected so in brackets]: between a karshina and a lentil there is only a little [difference].

messages.text: With regard to the statement of Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Yehuda: If the ear was pierced with a hole like the size of a lentil, then yes, it is considered a blemish, but if it was pierced with a hole less than the size of a lentil, then is it not considered a blemish? And one can raise a contradiction from a baraita:
messages.quote: Like the size of a lentil

messages.text: The Torah provides a description of the process by which a Hebrew slave who has already completed his six years of servitude may continue on as a slave of his master: “And you shall take the awl and put it through his ear and in the door.” From this verse, I have derived only that an awl can be used. From where do I know to include the palm thorn [hassol], a thorn, a needle, and a gimlet, and a stylus for writing on wax as valid tools for piercing his ear?

verse.he: וְלָקַחְתָּ אֶת־הַמַּרְצֵעַ וְנָתַתָּה בְאׇזְנוֹ וּבַדֶּלֶת וְהָיָה לְךָ עֶבֶד עוֹלָם וְאַף לַאֲמָתְךָ תַּעֲשֶׂה־כֵּן׃
verse.en: you shall take an awl and put it through their ear into the door, and they shall become your slave in perpetuity. Do this even with your female slave.

notes.he: קיסם שראשו חד שקורין ברוק"א:
notes.en: The sol: a sliver with a sharp point, which is called (Rashi adds an Old French gloss).

notes.he: קוץ:
notes.en: Sira: a thorn.

notes.he: טריבל"א:
notes.en: The makdei’aḥ [gimlet]: (Rashi adds an Old French gloss).

notes.he: עט ברזל:
notes.en: The mikhtav [stylus]: an iron pen.

notes.he: בלע"ז ברוקא:
notes.en: The sol: (Rabbeinu Gershom adds an Old French gloss).

messages.text: Therefore, the verse states: “And you shall take,” which indicates that anything that can be taken by hand is a valid tool. This is the statement of Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Yehuda.

notes.he: בפרק קמא דקדושין (דף כא:) מפרש משום דדריש ריבויי ומיעוטי ולקחת ריבה מרצע מיעט ונתת באזנו חזר וריבה מאי רבי רבי כל מילי מאי מיעט מיעט סם ותימה דמולקחת מרבינן כל דבר הנלקח ביד ואם סם לא מקרי נלקח ביד למה לי ריבה ומיעט וריבה מלשון ולקחת לחוד לא מתרבי אלא דבר הנלקח ביד וי"ל דמלשון ולקחת לא דריש אלא הכי קאמר לרבות כל דבר הנלקח ביד משום דדרשינן ריבויי ומיעוטי:
notes.en: To include anything taken by hand: in the first chapter of Kiddushin (21b) it explains [that this is] because he expounds amplifications and restrictions: “and you shall take” amplified, “awl” restricted, “through his ear” amplified again. What did it amplify? It amplified everything. What did it restrict? It restricted a caustic drug. And it is puzzling: if from “and you shall take” we include anything taken by hand, and a drug is not called “taken by hand,” why do I need amplification, restriction and amplification? From the wording “and you shall take” alone, only something taken by hand would be included! One can answer: he does not expound it from the wording “and you shall take”; rather, this is what it means: [it serves] to include anything taken by hand, because we expound amplifications and restrictions.

messages.text: Not all these items can be used. Rather, since the verse specifies an “awl,” only items similar to an awl can be used; just as an awl is distinct in that it is fashioned of metal, so too, anything fashioned of metal can be used.

notes.he: ובפ"ק דקדושין מפרש פלוגתייהו דרבי דריש כללי ופרטי ור' יוסי דריש ריבויי ומיעוטי:
notes.en: So too, anything of metal: and in the first chapter of Kiddushin [21b] it explains their dispute: Rabbi expounds [by the rule of] generalizations and details, and Rabbi Yosei expounds [by the rule of] amplifications and restrictions.

messages.text: And the latter clause of the baraita teaches:
When they pierce the ear of the slave, they pierce only in the earlobe.
messages.lead: Rabbi Elazar said that Yudan the Distinguished would teach as follows:

notes.he: אדם גדול:
notes.en: Beribbi: a great man.

messages.text: The Aramaic here reads only “Rabbi said”; the name Elazar is supplied by the Davidson English.

The piercing is not performed on that part of the ear, since there is a tradition that the ear of a Hebrew slave who is a priest is not pierced, because the piercing renders him blemished and unfit to serve in the Temple.

notes.he: בבשר שתחת האוזן הא אין רוצעין אלא בגובה של האוזן בסחוס ושם נעשה בעל מום הכהן וקא מרבי ר' יוסי אפי' מחט לרציעה ובהכי הוי בעל מום (עבר עבדי) [עבד עברי] כהן אלמא דבנקב בציר מכעדשה הוי מומא:
notes.en: Only in the milat: in the flesh beneath the ear. Rather, they pierce only in the upper part of the ear, in the cartilage, and there the priest becomes blemished. And Rabbi Yosei includes even a needle for the piercing, and with it a Hebrew slave who is a priest becomes blemished [the printed text garbles “Hebrew slave”; it is corrected in brackets]. Evidently a hole smaller than a lentil is a blemish.

messages.text: And if you say that they pierced the slave in the earlobe, how does a Hebrew slave who is a priest become blemished through piercing? A wound on this part of the ear heals. This indicates that they pierce only on the upper part of the ear, through the cartilage.

notes.he: אליה:
notes.en: In the milat: the lobe.

notes.he: הא הדר בריא:
notes.en: How does he become blemished?: it heals!

notes.he: בניחותא. הא ודאי אין רוצעין אלא בגובה של אוזן שהוא סחוס ומכל מקום קשיא דקתני הכא דמן הרציעה נעשה בעל מום וקאמר רבי יוסי ברבי יהודה דרציעה ישנה במחט דלא הוי כעדשה:
notes.en: Rather, they pierce only: [read] as a statement [not a question]. Certainly they pierce only in the upper part of the ear, which is cartilage. And in any case it is difficult, for it teaches here that the piercing makes him blemished, and Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Yehuda says that piercing can be done with a needle, [whose hole] is not as large as a lentil.

messages.caption: The two parts of the ear on this daf, as a plain schematic: the cartilage above and the soft lobe (“skin”) below.

messages.text: In any event, it is clear from the statement of Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Yehuda, that the piercing of a needle is considered a blemish, despite the fact that it is definitely smaller than the size of a lentil.

It is not difficult, as here, Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Yehuda, said that the hole must be the size of a lentil with regard to slaughtering an animal outside the Temple due to the blemish. There, with regard to disqualifying the animal from being sacrificed, even a tiny hole is considered a blemish, just as it renders the priest blemished.
messages.quote: the piercing of a needle is considered a blemish

notes.he: יש מומין הרבה בבכור שפוסלים אותו ליקרב על גבי מזבח ואין מכשירין אותו לישחט כדתנן אלו שאין שוחטין עליהן לא במקדש ולא במדינה כו':
notes.en: Here for slaughtering, there for disqualifying: there are many blemishes in a firstborn that disqualify it from being offered on the altar but do not make it fit to be slaughtered, as we learned: “These are [the blemishes] for which one does not slaughter, neither in the Temple nor in the country,” etc. [41a].

notes.he: מדפסיל כהן משמע דהוי מום דאורייתא ושמא האי דאין שוחטין משום דאין ניכר יפה וגזרינן אטו מומין שבסתר אי נמי האי דמפסיל כהן משום דאינו שוה בזרעו של אהרן א"נ מום עובר הוא ובעינן שלא יפסל אפילו לפי שעה משום דכתיב [ושב] אל משפחתו דדרשי' בקדושין (שם) למותר שבמשפחתו:
notes.en: Here for slaughtering, there for disqualifying: since it disqualifies a priest, it implies that it is a Torah-level blemish. And perhaps the reason one does not slaughter [for it] is that it is not clearly visible, and we decree on account of hidden blemishes. Alternatively, the reason it disqualifies a priest is that he is not equal among Aaron’s offspring. Alternatively, it is a temporary blemish, and we require that he not be disqualified even temporarily, since it is written: “[And he shall return] to his family,” which we expound in Kiddushin (ibid.) [to mean]: to that which is permitted in his family [i.e., to his family’s standing].

notes.he: עליו הבכור אינו נשחט אלא על נקב כעדשה:
notes.en: It is not difficult; here for slaughtering: for this, the firstborn is slaughtered only for a hole the size of a lentil.

notes.he: להקרבה אפי' בנקב במחט הוי פסול:
notes.en: There for disqualifying: from being sacrificed, even a hole [made] by a needle disqualifies.

messages.text: § According to the first opinion cited in the baraita, the size of the hole that is considered a blemish in the ear of the firstborn animal is like that of a karshina. What is a karshina?
It is a bitter vetch, called hinda in Aramaic.

notes.he: בלשון זה היו מכירין ובלשון לע"ז ויצ"א:
notes.en: Hinda: by this name they knew it; and in the vernacular (Rashi adds an Old French gloss).

notes.he: במקומו קורין לכרשינה הינדא:
notes.en: Hinda: in his place they call a karshina “hinda.”

messages.text: @Rav Huna Is this measure referring to a bitter vetch that can enter and exit the hole in the ear, which means that the hole is slightly larger than the bitter vetch? Or is it referring to a bitter vetch that is stationary in the hole, meaning that the hole is precisely the size of a bitter vetch?
messages.lead: With regard to this halakha, Rav Hoshaya asked Rav Huna the Great:

notes.he: העומד בנקב בדוחק ואע"פ שאינה נכנסת (עמו) ויוצאת בו הוי מום או דלמא לא הוי מום עד שיהא הנקב רחב שכרשינה תהא נכנסת ויוצאת בו:
notes.en: Karshina: [is it one] that stands tightly in the hole, so that even though it does not enter and exit through it, it is a blemish? Or perhaps it is not a blemish until the hole is wide enough for a karshina to enter and exit through it?

notes.he: כרשינה העומדת בדוחק בנקב או נכנסת ויוצאה בריוח:
notes.en: A karshina that stands tightly in the hole, or that enters and exits freely?

messages.text: @Rav Oshaya I did not hear this halakha specifically, but I heard a similar halakha to it, that the expression: The size of a bitter vetch [melo karshina], means that the bitter vetch can enter and exit the hole.
messages.quote: a bitter vetch that can enter and exit

notes.he: מסיפא נפקא לן דקאמר מקדח וחיסומו שנינו דהיינו נכנס ויוצא:
notes.en: I heard [a ruling] similar to it: we derive it from the end [of the passage], where he says: “We learned: a drill and its obstruction,” which means entering and exiting [38a].

messages.text: The spine and the skull of a corpse that are incomplete do not impart ritual impurity in a tent. This halakha was unanimously accepted, but the details were subject to dispute: How much is considered a deficiency in the spine so that it will not impart impurity in a tent? Beit Shammai say: If it is missing two vertebrae, and Beit Hillel say: Even if it is missing only one vertebra, it will not impart impurity.

notes.he: שלימין מטמאין באהל ושאר עצמות אין מטמאין באהל וכמה יחסרו ולא יטמאו:
notes.en: The spine and the skull: when whole, they impart impurity in a tent, while other bones do not impart impurity in a tent. And how much must they be lacking so that they do not impart impurity?

notes.he: כמה חסרון בשדרה שלא תטמא באהל:
notes.en: How much deficiency in the spine, so that it does not impart impurity in a tent?

messages.text: And likewise, they disagree concerning the deficiency in the skull: Beit Shammai say that it must be missing a piece like the size of a drilled hole, and Beit Hillel say: It must be missing an amount that if removed from a living person, he would die.

notes.he: ובכמלא מקדח וימות לב"ש כדקאמר בפ"ק דעירובין (דף ז.) וכן לטרפה ומשמע דאתרוייהו קאי אשדרה ואגולגולת אלא ב"ה אתו למימר דשיעורו כמלא מקדח הוי טפי מכדי שינטל מן החי וימות לדידהו ורבינו תם נמי דמפרש דלא קאי וכן לטרפה אגולגולת מדלא פריך בריש אלו טריפות (חולין דף מב:) והאיכא כמה חסרון בגולגולת כדפריך מחסרון בשדרה משום דבנקיבת הקרום הוי טריפה בלא חסרון והא דקרי בעירובין (דף ז.) שדרה וגולגולת תרי חומרי דסתרי אהדדי משום דהוו פליגי גבי טריפות דאדם דאית ליה מזלא ואית ליה טפי חיות ולא מיטרף בנקיבת קרום בלא חסרון עמו מ"מ לפירושו נמי צ"ל כן כמו שפירשנו דבשיעורא דב"ש ימות (לב"ש) כמו לב"ה בשיעורא דידהו ומיהו מה שמדקדק ר"ת מדלא פריך בריש אלו טריפות (חולין דף מב:) מחסרון דגולגולת לאו פירכא הוא דמצינן למימר דטריפות של חסרון לא הוי אלא משום דסופו של קרום לינקב כמו ריאה דדמיא לדיותא : ולכוחלא (שם מז:) ועוד קשה לפי שמחלק בין דאדם לטרפות דבהמות דבריש אלו טריפות (חולין מג.) מ להו דפריך להו מאיוב ישפוך לארץ מרירתי ועדיין איוב קיים ומיהו הוה יכול ר"ת לפרש דלא מטעם מזלא חשיב טריפה בבהמה טפי מאדם אלא כגון דניקב קרום של מוח העליון ולא התחתון ובבהמה קרום התחתון רך ואין מגין על המוח אבל באדם התחתון קשה ומגין משום הכי בעי חסרון עם נקיבת העליון אבל בדבר ששוין בזה ובזה אין לחלק ביניהם כלל:
notes.en: In brief: Tosafot explain, citing the first chapter of Eruvin (7a), that by Beit Shammai’s measure, a drill’s hole, the person would also die, and that the same applies to tereifa; the measures refer to both the spine and the skull, and Beit Hillel come to say that by their view a drill’s hole is more than “enough that if removed from a living person he would die.” They discuss Rabbeinu Tam, who explains that “and likewise for tereifa” does not refer to the skull, since at the beginning of Elu Tereifot (Ḥullin 42b) the Gemara objects from a deficiency in the spine but not from one in the skull (a perforated brain membrane alone makes an animal tereifa, without any deficiency), and who explains that Eruvin (7a) calls the rulings on the spine and the skull two contradictory stringencies because they disagreed over tereifa in a person, who is more resilient and is not rendered tereifa by a perforated membrane without a deficiency. Even by his explanation, Tosafot say, one must explain as they did, that at Beit Shammai’s measure he dies, as at Beit Hillel’s. They reject his proof from Ḥullin: a deficiency may render an animal tereifa only because the membrane will eventually be perforated, like a lung that looks like ink or kohl (Ḥullin 47b). They also question his distinction between people and animals from Ḥullin (43a), where the Gemara objects from Job (“He pours out my gall upon the ground,” and Job lived), and suggest he could have explained instead that the case is a perforated upper membrane only: in an animal the lower membrane is soft and does not protect the brain, while in a person it is hard and protects it, so a person needs a deficiency as well; but where the two are alike, there is no distinction at all. Open on Sefaria for the full text.

messages.text: That which was stated: An amount that if removed from a living person, how much is that?
messages.lead: And Rav Ḥisda was sitting, and he raised a dilemma:
messages.quote: an amount that if removed from a living person, he would die

notes.he: ה"ג ויתיב רב חסדא וקמיבעיא ליה ואיתמר רב ספרא אמר שמעתא א"ל רב תחליפא לרב חסדא דהכי אתנייה שמואל:
notes.en: This is the reading: “And Rav Ḥisda was sitting and raising a dilemma …” and “It was stated: Rav Safra said: [It was] a shmaata [an amoraic statement] that Rav Taḥlifa said to Rav Ḥisda, that thus Shmuel taught him.”

messages.text: @Rav Ḥisda It is like the size of a sela coin.
And it was stated that the amora’im disagreed with regard to whom Rav Taḥlifa cited when relating this halakha to Rav Ḥisda.
He told him a halakha of the amora’im citing Shmuel.

notes.he: שמעתא כלומר מימרא הא דשמואל:
notes.en: And likewise in the skull. Shmaata: that is, a statement, this one of Shmuel.

messages.text: He told him a baraita that stipulated that the measure is like the size of a sela coin.

And your mnemonic to remember what each one said is the common talmudic phrase: Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda teaches [tanei], generally indicating a source from a tanna, which hints that according to Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda, Rav Taḥlifa cited a baraita to Rav Ḥisda, while according to Rav Safra, he related a tradition from Shmuel.

notes.he: שלא תטעה מי אמר שמעתא ומי מתניתא תני רב יהודה בר שמואל דאשכחן מקומות הרבה בש"ס דאיירי רב שמואל בר יהודה בל' מתניתא תני רב שמואל בר יהודה במסכת ע"ז רפואות דאין מעמידין (דף כח:):
notes.en: And your mnemonic: so that you do not err as to who said “a shmaata” and who [said] “a baraita”: “Rav Yehuda bar Shmuel teaches” [so Rashi’s text reads here; he goes on to name Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda], for we find in many places in the Talmud that Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda speaks in the language of a baraita: “Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda taught,” in tractate Avoda Zara, [in the passage on] remedies, in chapter Ein Ma’amidin (28b).

notes.he: וסימניך לגירסא דרב יהודה אמר מתניתא דמשכחת טובא דתני רב שמואל בר יהודה ומתניתא הוי עיקר:
notes.en: And your mnemonic, for the reading: “Rav Yehuda said: a baraita” [so Rabbeinu Gershom’s text]: for we often find “Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda taught,” and the baraita [version] is the main one.

messages.text: @Rav Taḥlifa bar Avudimi If so, that the measure of the deficiency according to the opinion of Beit Hillel is the size of a sela coin, you have made the statement of Beit Shammai and the statement of Beit Hillel one and the same, since the size of a sela coin and a drilled hole is identical. As we learned in a mishna:
messages.quote: It is like the size of a sela coin

notes.he: רב חסדא לרב תחליפא:
notes.en: And he said to him: Rav Ḥisda to Rav Taḥlifa.

notes.he: דבית הלל כסלע אמר עשית ב"ש וב"ה אחד:
notes.en: If so: that Beit Hillel said “like a sela,” you have made Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel one.

notes.he: רב חסדא א"כ כדקאמרת בסלע עשית דברי ב"ש וב"ה אחד כדתנן מאור שלא נעשה בידי אדם כגון כותל שבין ב' בתים ובבית אחד טומאה ובאותו כותל יש נקב כמין חלון שנעשה מאיליו כגון אבן שנקובה מאיליה שיעורו של אותו נקב אם הוא כמו אגרוף גדול מביא את הטומאה מבית לבית ומיטמאין אדם וכלים שבבית אחר. ואם המאור הוא פחות מיכן חוצץ בפני הטומאה:
notes.en: He said to him: Rav Ḥisda [said]: If so, as you say, a sela, you have made the words of Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel one, as we learned: A window not made by human hands, for example a wall between two houses, with impurity in one house, and in that wall there is a hole like a window that came about by itself, for example a stone that became perforated by itself: the measure of that hole, if it is like a large fist, brings the impurity from house to house, and the people and vessels in the other house become impure. And if the window is less than this, it blocks the impurity.

messages.text: With regard to a window that was not fashioned by the hands of a person, such as where a stone fell out of the wall by itself, its measure for which ritual impurity is transmitted from room to room is like the size of a large fist. And this is the size of the fist of Ben Avatiaḥ, who was known to be an exceptionally large man.

notes.he: חלון שלא נעשה בידי אדם שנפל הכותל מאליו מעט בין בית לבית:
notes.en: A window: an opening not made by human hands, where the wall between one house and another fell away a little by itself.

notes.he: להביא טומאה מבית זה לבית זה:
notes.en: Its measure: for bringing impurity from this house to that house.

notes.he: דכיון דלא נעשה בידי אדם בציר מהכי לא חשיב:
notes.en: The size of a large fist: since it was not made by human hands, anything less than this is not significant.

notes.he: שם האיש בעל בשר:
notes.en: Ben Avatiaḥ: the name of a man who was very fleshy.

notes.he: בן אחותו של רבן יוחנן בן זכאי שהיה איש גדול ביותר:
notes.en: The fist of Ben Batiaḥ: the son of the sister of Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai, who was an exceptionally large man.

messages.text: And the size of this fist is like the size of a large human head.

notes.he: לאותו אגרוף:
notes.en: And it is: [the size of] that fist.

notes.he: שיעור של אותו אגרוף כראש גדול:
notes.en: And it is: the measure of that fist is like a large head.

messages.text: But if the window was made by the hand of a person, its measure for which ritual impurity is transmitted is like the size of the drilled hole of the large drill of the chamber in the Temple, which is like the size of the Italian pundeyon and like the size of a sela of the emperor Nero. And its size is…

notes.he: שמונח בלשכה לקדוח את הצריך לבדק הבית:
notes.en: Of the chamber: that was kept in the chamber for drilling whatever was needed for the Temple’s upkeep.

notes.he: כלומר לזה ולזה דומה:
notes.en: Like the Italian pundeyon and like a Neronian sela: that is, it resembles both this and that.

notes.he: לאותו סלע ולאותו פונדיון:
notes.en: And it is: [the size of] that sela and that pundeyon.

notes.he: ומאור שנעשה בידי אדם שנקב שיעורו אם הוא כמלא מקדח גדול של לשכה כמקדח גדול שבלשכה מביא את הטומאה וכיון שעשוי בידי אדם במתכוין סגי בבציר שיעורא אלמא דמקדח נמי הוי כסלע א"כ מה בין ב"ש וב"ה בגלגלת:
notes.en: And a window that was made by human hands, that someone drilled: its measure, if it is the size of the large drill of the chamber, like the large drill that was in the chamber, it brings the impurity; and since it was made by human hands intentionally, a smaller measure suffices. Evidently, the drill too is like a sela; if so, what is [the difference] between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel regarding the skull?

messages.text: The mishna from Kelim, and Rav Ḥisda’s challenge to Rav Taḥlifa, continue on 38a.
